Reports published with at least one recommendation that mentions "suicide" (data as of 2026-11-04, not stale):

| Year | Reports with a suicide recommendation | Suicide recommendations | All reports with recommendations | All recommendations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | 56 | 98 | 180 | 878 |
| 2025 | 11 | 19 | 155 | 775 |

The count fell from 56 to 11 reports. As a share of reports with recommendations, it fell from about 31% (56 of 180) to about 7% (11 of 155). So this data does not show suicide prevention growing as an OIG theme. On these counts it shrank.

**What the counts can show**
- How many published reports carry a recommendation containing the word "suicide", and how that changed between the two years.
- The drop is large. It is much bigger than the small change in total reports (180 to 155) or total recommendations (878 to 775).

**What they cannot show**
- **Why it fell.** A fall could mean OIG's attention shifted. It could also mean inspection protocols or report formats changed, or that facilities had fewer suicide-related problems. These counts cannot tell those apart.
- **The 2025 figure may be incomplete.** Of the 2025 suicide recommendations, 6 of 19 are still open. Nothing in the data says all 2025 reports are in yet. I also did not check whether OIG's recommendation-writing pattern differs between years.
- **Keyword matching is crude.** The count misses recommendations that cover suicide prevention without the word "suicide", such as "safety planning" or "lethal means". It also includes recommendations where suicide is only mentioned in passing. It counts recommendations, not reports' overall content. Reports with findings but no recommendations are excluded.
- **Topic coverage.** I did not use OIG's "Suicide Prevention" topic tag. OIG tagged only about a quarter of reports, so it would undercount.
- **Two years is not a trend.** Two data points cannot establish a trend. A check of earlier years would be needed to know whether 2024 was a peak or 2025 a dip.

I can run the same count for earlier years, or split it by report type, to test whether the drop comes from a change in the inspection program.

**The median for VBA recommendations is 179 days.** The middle half of them closed between about 134 and 312 days after the report was published (the first and third quartiles).

**What it measures:** the days from a report's publication to the closure date shown on VA OIG's site. The closure date appears to record when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing evidence. That can come months after VBA actually did the work, so the figure is not how long VBA took to fix the problem.

**Details**
- **Sample:** 923 of VBA's 966 recommendations are closed. The median uses 914 of them. The other 9 have no closure date. 43 VBA recommendations are still open, so they are not in the median.
- **Closed on publication day:** 110 recommendations were closed the day the report came out, presumably because the action was done beforehand. This pulls the median down.
- **Not implemented:** 26 of the closed recommendations (2.8%) were closed as not implemented.
- **Open items:** the median age of open items is 161 days. 17 have been open over a year, and the oldest has been open 1,567 days.
- **Counting:** a recommendation that names two offices counts for both.
- **Target dates:** the data can't show whether VBA met its target dates. A target date is the facility's own estimate, and a closure after it doesn't show a missed commitment.

Source: VA OIG recommendations data (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all), data as of 2026-11-04. The data is not stale.

Data is as of 2026-11-04 and isn't stale. Here are two examples of what facilities committed to do after OIG cited them for unsecured medication carts.

**1. Atlanta VA Medical Center, report 13-03653-91** (published 2014-03-12)
[Report link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-atlanta-va-1)
- OIG found that not all medication drawers were secured because of faulty locking mechanisms.
- Nursing staff committed to keeping carts secured at all times.
- They would repair or replace carts without working locks. Six replacement carts had arrived and 26 more were on order.
- Until then, carts would be kept in a locked medication room unless in use.
- The Bar Code Medication Administration (BCMA) Coordinator would round on all inpatient areas and document compliance.
- The target date was 12/31/2014. The recommendation is closed-implemented, with a closure date of 2015-03-11.

**2. San Francisco VA Health Care System, report 15-00607-483** (published 2015-08-24)
[Report link](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-san-4)
- All the carts have automatic timed lockouts. Staff were told to physically lock carts and not rely on the automatic timeout.
- Charge Nurses and Nurse Managers would do random checks through the day.
- The Unit Charge Nurse would complete daily Environment of Care rounds. The daily log would be reported at the monthly Nursing Division meeting and included in the minutes.
- The target date was 9/30/2015. The recommendation is closed-implemented, with a closure date of 2016-04-07.

Both examples come from older inspection reports. Other reports, such as Battle Creek (15-00606-495) and Palo Alto (13-00279-156), show similar commitments to staff re-education and audits until compliance reached 100%.
